newsitem.title: USA: House debates giving private workers more comp time.
newsitem.headline: House debates giving private workers more comp time.

text.p: The House Wednesday debated a Republican proposal to let workers take time off rather than overtime pay if they racked up extra hours, but President Clinton threatened to veto the measure without major changes.

In a letter to House Speaker Newt Gingrich, Clinton said he supported efforts to help working parents spend more time with their families, but he charged the Republican bill did not provide adequate protection for employees and would undermine longstanding fair labour laws.

"I intend to veto any legislation that fails to guarantee real choice for employees, real protection against employer abuse and preservation of fair labour standards such as the 40-hour work week," Clinton said.

The Working Families Flexibility Act is a top priority of congressional Republicans, who say it will give working parents more opportunity to spend time with their children or care for a sick relative. But it is adamantly opposed by organised labour, an important source of campaign donations for Democrats.

The measure would allow private-sector businesses to give workers the choice of taking 1-1/2 hours of paid time off, called comp time, instead of time-and-a-half pay, for every hour of overtime worked. Any comp time agreement would have to be voluntary and workers would be able to withdraw.

Employees who work for hourly wages rather than an annual salary are covered by the 1938 Fair Labour Standards Act, which requires time-and-a-half overtime after 40 hours in one week. About 57 percent of the work force is covered by the act but Congress has voted to give public sector employees the ability to opt for comp time instead of pay.

Republicans angrily denied Democratic charges that workers would be subject to abuse under the bill, saying they had built in protections to ensure employers did not coerce workers to take comp time or abuse the new flexibility.

"These are the American people we're talking about. This legislation says to the American worker, you make the decision," Pennsylvania Republican Representative William Goodling, a chief author of the measure, said. "It's totally demeaning to be talking as if American workers can't make choices ... An employer would be a fool if they tried to intimidate an employee."
Democrats charged that workers would have little say in using their comp time because employers could deny a request to take time off if it disrupted the operations of the business.

If a firm went out of business, they said, there would be no protection for workers who had accrued a large amount of comp time. They also said ending the federal requirement for overtime eroded the principle of the 40-hour work week.

"(The bill) is nothing but a Trojan horse designed to fool workers into believing the majority has experienced some kind of pro-worker, gender-friendly epiphany," Missouri Democratic Representative William Clay said.
Clinton has proposed amending the Family and Medical Leave law, which allows many workers to take leave for family matters, to give working parents more flexibility.

The vote on the bill was expected to be close. Democrats planned to offer a substitute setting more stringent requirements for comp time and Republicans were expected to offer a series of amendments to soften the legislation, including reducing the amount of compensatory time that could be accured to 160 hours from 240 hours.
